source_text:
Ceterum de incendio mundi, aut inprouisum ignem cadere aut † difficile, non credere uulgaris erroris est.
quis enim sapientium dubitat, quis ignorat, omnia quae orta sunt, occidere, quae facta sunt, interire? caelum quoque cum omnibus quae caelo continentur, ita ut coepit, si desierit fontium dulcis aqua maria nutrire, in uim ignis abiturum, Stoicis constans opinio est, quod consumto umore mundus hic omnis ignescat.
et Epicureis de elementorum conflagratione et mundi ruina eadem ipsa sententia est...
loquitur Plato: partes orbis nunc inundare dicit, nunc alternis uicibus ardescere, et cum ipsum mundum perpetuum et insolubilem diceret esse fabricatum, addidit tamen, ipsi artifici Deo soli et solubilem et esse mortalem.
ita nihil mirum est, si ista moles ab eo, quo exgtructa est, destruatur. animaduertis philosophos eadem disputare quae dicimus, non quod nos simus eorum uestigia subsecuti, sed quod illi de diuinis praedictionibus profetarum umbram interpolatae ueritatis imitati sint.
sic etiam condicionem renascendi sapientium clariores, Pythagoras primus et praecipuus Plato, corrupta et dimidiata fide tradiderunt: nam corporibus dissolutis
solas animas uolunt et perpetuo manere et in alia noua corpora saepius commeare.
addunt istis et illa ad retorquendam ueritatem, in pecudes, aues, beluas hominum animas redire. non philosophi sane studio, sed mimi conuicio digna ista sententia est:
sed ad propositum satis est, etiam in hoc sapientes uestros in aliquem modum nobiscum consonare.
ceterum quis tam stultus aut brutus est, ut audeat repugnare, hominem a Deo, ut primum potuisse fingi, ita posse denuo reformari? nihil esse post obitum, et ante ortum nihil fuisse? sicut de nihilo nasci licuit, ita de nihilo licere reparari? porro difficilius est, id quod non sit incipere, quam id quod fuerit iterare. tu perire et Deo credis, si quid oculis nostris hebetibus subtrahitur? corpus omne siue arescit in puluerem siue in umorem soluitur uel in cinerem comprimitur uel in nidorem\'. tenuatur, subducitur nobis, sed Deo elementorum custodi reseruatur. nec, ut creditis, ullum damnum sepulturae timemus, sed ueterem et meliorem consuetudinem humandi frequentamus.
uide adeo, quam in solacium nostri resurrectionem futuram omnis natura meditetur. sol demergit et nascitur, astra labuntur et redeunt, flores occidunt et reuiuescunt, post senium arbusta frondescunt, semina nonnisi corrupta reuirescunt: ita corpus in sepulcro, ut arbores in hiberno: occultant uirorem ariditate mentita.
\' quid festinas, ut cruda adhuc hieme reuiuescat et redeat? expectandum nobis etiam corporis uer est. nec ignoro plerosque conscientia meritorum nihil se esse post mortem magis optare quam credere: malunt enim extingui penitus quam ad supplicia reparari. quorum error augetur et in saeculo libertate remissa et Dei patientia maxima, cuius quanto iudicium tardum, tanto magis iustum est.
thought_title: The world's end and the body's resurrection
orientation: Octavius is replying to Caecilius, arguing that even pagan philosophers agree the world will end by fire and that the body can be remade by God.
pass_a_gloss: But about the burning of the world, to not believe that fire falls either unforeseen or with difficulty is the mark of common error. For who of the wise doubts, who does not know, that all things which have arisen pass away, that all things which have been made perish? The heaven too, with all things which are contained in heaven, just as it began, if the sweet water of the springs should cease to nourish the seas, will pass into the force of fire; this is the fixed opinion of the Stoics, that when the moisture is consumed this whole world catches fire. And for the Epicureans there is the same very opinion about the burning up of the elements and the ruin of the world. Plato speaks: he says that parts of the world are now flooded, now in turn blaze up, and although he said that the world itself was made everlasting and indissoluble, he added nevertheless that to its maker God alone it is both dissoluble and mortal. So it is no wonder if this mass is destroyed by him by whom it was built. You notice that the philosophers discuss the same things which we say, not because we have followed their footsteps, but because they have imitated the shadow of interpolated truth from the divine predictions of the prophets. So also the more famous of the wise, Pythagoras first and especially Plato, handed down the condition of being reborn with a corrupted and halved faith: for when bodies are dissolved they wish that souls alone both remain forever and pass over repeatedly into other new bodies. They add to these also those things for twisting back the truth, that the souls of humans return into cattle, birds, beasts. That opinion is worthy not of the zeal of a philosopher but of the mockery of a mime. But for the purpose at hand it is enough that even in this your wise men agree with us in some manner. But who is so foolish or brutish that he dares to fight against it, that a human being, just as he could first be fashioned by God, so can be formed again anew? That there is nothing after death, and that there was nothing before birth? Just as it was permitted to be born from nothing, so it is permitted to be restored from nothing? Further, it is more difficult for that which does not exist to begin than for that which has existed to be repeated. Do you believe that it perishes and is lost to God, if anything is withdrawn from our dull eyes? Every body, whether it dries into dust or dissolves into moisture or is pressed into ash or is thinned into vapor, is withdrawn from us, but is kept for God, the guardian of the elements. Nor, as you believe, do we fear any loss from burial, but we practice the old and better custom of burying. See indeed how all nature meditates on the resurrection that is to be for our consolation. The sun sinks and is born, the stars slip away and return, flowers die and revive, after old age trees grow leaves again, seeds do not grow green again unless corrupted: so the body in the tomb, as trees in winter: they hide their greenness with a feigned dryness. Why do you hurry, that it should revive and return while winter is still raw? We must wait also for the spring of the body. Nor am I ignorant that very many, because of consciousness of their deserts, wish rather than believe that they are nothing after death: for they prefer to be utterly extinguished than to be restored for punishments. Their error is increased both by the license relaxed in this age and by the very great patience of God, whose judgment, the slower it is, the more just it is.

choices.english: fire falls either unforeseen or with difficulty
choices.why: The text is damaged; I render the visible words literally and note the corruption.
rejected: fire falls unforeseen or hard to believe

choices.why: Keeps the metaphor of a shadow and the idea that the philosophers' truth has been tampered with or inserted.
rejected: a shadow of the truth they had corrupted

choices.why: Condicio here means the state or condition, not a command; the gerund keeps the abstract sense.

choices.english: with a corrupted and halved faith
choices.why: Dimidiata means cut in half, which fits Octavius's point that they got only part of the truth.
rejected: with a faith corrupted and divided

choices.why: Conuicium is abuse or mockery; mime fits the theatrical insult Octavius intends.
Custos as guardian keeps the idea that God watches over the material elements of the body.

pass_b_english: As for the burning of the world, to refuse to believe that fire falls either unforeseen or with difficulty is a common error. Who among the wise doubts, who does not know, that everything which has arisen passes away, and everything which has been made is destroyed? The Stoics hold it as a settled opinion that the sky too, with everything contained in the sky, will pass into the force of fire just as it began, if the sweet water of the springs should cease to nourish the seas; because when the moisture is consumed, this whole world catches fire. The Epicureans hold the same view about the burning up of the elements and the ruin of the world. Plato speaks: he says that parts of the world are now flooded, now burn in alternating turns, and although he said that the world itself was made perpetual and indissoluble, he nevertheless added that for God its maker alone it is both dissoluble and mortal. So it is no wonder if this mass is destroyed by the one by whom it was built. You notice that the philosophers discuss the same things we say, not because we have followed in their footsteps, but because they have imitated the shadow of interpolated truth from the divine predictions of the prophets.

So also the more distinguished of the wise, Pythagoras first and chiefly Plato, handed down the condition of being reborn with a corrupted and halved faith: for when bodies are dissolved, they claim that souls alone remain forever and often pass over into other new bodies. To twist the truth, they add this too: that the souls of humans return into cattle, birds, and beasts. That view deserves not the serious study of a philosopher but the mockery of a mime. But for our purpose it is enough that even in this your wise men agree with us in some measure.

For who is so foolish or brutish as to dare to deny that a human being, since he could first be formed by God, can also be formed again? That there is nothing after death, and that there was nothing before birth? Just as it was possible to be born from nothing, so it is possible to be restored from nothing. Indeed, it is more difficult for what does not exist to begin than for what has existed to be repeated. Do you believe that anything is lost to God if it is withdrawn from our dull eyes? Every body, whether it dries into dust or dissolves into moisture or is pressed into ash or thinned into vapor, is withdrawn from us, but it is preserved for God, the guardian of the elements. Nor do we fear, as you believe, any loss from burial; rather, we practice the old and better custom of interment.

See, indeed, how all nature meditates on the resurrection that will be for our comfort. The sun sinks and is born again, the stars glide away and return, flowers die and revive, trees grow green again after old age, seeds do not grow green again unless they are corrupted: so the body in the tomb is like trees in winter: they hide their greenness with a pretended dryness. Why are you in a hurry for it to revive and return while winter is still raw? We must wait for the spring of the body as well. Nor am I unaware that many, conscious of their deserts, prefer to be nothing after death rather than to believe: they would rather be utterly extinguished than restored for punishment. Their error is increased both by the license allowed in this world and by God's great patience, whose judgment is the more just the slower it is.
notes: The phrase 'aut inprouisum ignem cadere aut † difficile' contains a textual corruption marked by the dagger; the word after 'aut' is uncertain. I have glossed the visible words and noted the damage.

problems.quote: prefer to believe that they are nothing after death rather than to hope
problems.why: Latin says they prefer the belief that nothing exists after death rather than belief, no mention of 'hope'.
problems.fix: prefer to believe that they are nothing after death rather than to believe

problems.quote: whose judgment is as just as it is slow
problems.source_quote: cuius quanto iudicium tardum, tanto magis iustum est
problems.fix: whose judgment is the more just the slower it is
problems.ruling: "quanto ... tanto" means "the more ... the more", not simple equality "as ... as".

edits.old: prefer to believe that they are nothing after death rather than to hope
edits.new: prefer to believe that they are nothing after death rather than to believe

edits.old: whose judgment is as just as it is slow
edits.new: whose judgment is the more just the slower it is

fixed: Changed 'rather than to hope' to 'rather than to believe': source 'magis optare quam credere' means they prefer (wish) to believe nothing exists after death rather than to believe (in resurrection); no mention of hope.

Changed 'as just as it is slow' to 'the more just the slower it is': source 'quanto iudicium tardum, tanto magis iustum est' is a correlative construction meaning 'the slower the judgment, the more just it is.'

problems.quote: prefer to believe that they are nothing after death rather than to believe
problems.source_quote: magis optare quam credere: malunt enim extingui penitus quam ad supplicia reparari
problems.why: English adds an extra “to believe” and changes “prefer to be nothing after death” into “prefer to believe they are nothing”, altering the meaning.
problems.fix: prefer to think they are nothing after death rather than to believe (in the resurrection).

problems.quote: when the moisture is consumed, this whole world catches fire
problems.source_quote: quod consumto umore mundus hic omnis ignescat
problems.why: English 'when' makes this a temporal clause, but Latin 'quod' = 'because'—giving the reason for the Stoic opinion, not a temporal sequence.
problems.fix: because when the moisture is consumed, this whole world catches fire
problems.ruling: Latin causal ‘quod’, English temporal ‘when’ changes reason

edits.old: prefer to believe that they are nothing after death rather than to believe
edits.new: prefer to be nothing after death rather than to believe

edits.old: when the moisture is consumed, this whole world catches fire
edits.new: because when the moisture is consumed, this whole world catches fire

fixed: Changed 'prefer to believe that they are nothing after death rather than to believe' to 'prefer to be nothing after death rather than to believe': source 'magis optare quam credere' means 'wish rather than believe', so the English should say they prefer to be nothing, not prefer to believe they are nothing.
Changed 'when the moisture is consumed' to 'because when the moisture is consumed': source 'quod consumto umore' uses 'quod' as 'because', giving the reason for the Stoic opinion.

problems.quote: blind fortune or uncertain nature rules
problems.why: These terms shift between Caecilius's skeptical 'fortune/nature' and Octavius's theological 'fate' without clear distinction of who uses which.
problems.fix: Clarify that 'fate' is God's ordering, 'fortune' is blind chance.

problems.quote: Pythagoras first and chiefly Plato, handed down the condition of being reborn with a corrupted and halved faith
problems.why: 'corrupted and halved faith' is opaque; means 'imperfect/ partial belief in rebirth.'
problems.fix: 'a corrupted and partial faith' or 'imperfect belief'

edits.old: with a corrupted and halved faith
edits.new: with a corrupted and partial faith

fixed: The glossary problem about 'fate' and 'fortune' does not appear in this section; no such terms occur in the source or English here.
The phrase 'corrupted and halved faith' is opaque; the source 'corrupta et dimidiata fide' means a faith that is both corrupted and divided/incomplete, so 'partial' better renders 'dimidiata'.

last_rejected.quote: to refuse to believe that fire falls either unforeseen or with difficulty
last_rejected.source_quote: aut inprouisum ignem cadere aut † difficile, non credere uulgaris erroris est
last_rejected.why: Latin says refusing to believe fire falls unforeseen OR with difficulty is the error; English flips to 'refuse to believe...is a common error' without the 'or', and 'difficile' likely means 'with difficulty' as a corruption for 'deficere' or similar, but the English structure misrepresents the Latin claim about what constitutes the error.
last_rejected.fix: To believe that fire will not fall unforeseen or with difficulty upon the world is a common error.
last_rejected.ruling: English includes ‘either … or …’ matching Latin ‘aut … aut …’

last_rejected.quote: if the sweet water of the springs should cease to nourish the seas
last_rejected.source_quote: si desierit fontium dulcis aqua maria nutrire
last_rejected.why: The Latin says 'if the sweet water of springs should cease to nourish the seas' — the English inverts the relationship, making springs nourish seas rather than the waters ceasing to nourish.
last_rejected.fix: if the sweet water of springs should cease to nourish the seas
last_rejected.ruling: Both render springs’ sweet water ceasing to nourish the seas

last_rejected.quote: they claim that souls alone remain forever and often pass over into other new bodies
last_rejected.source_quote: solas animas uolunt et perpetuo manere et in alia noua corpora saepius commeare
last_rejected.why: 'solas animas' = souls alone (only souls, not bodies); 'perpetuo manere' = remain forever; 'saepius' = more often/repeatedly, not 'often'. The English misses 'solas' emphasis and mistranslates 'saepius'.
last_rejected.fix: they want souls alone both to remain forever and repeatedly to pass into other new bodies
last_rejected.ruling: Core meaning kept; ‘saepius’ vs ‘often’ is minor nuance

last_rejected.quote: To twist the truth, they add this too
last_rejected.source_quote: addunt istis et illa ad retorquendam ueritatem
last_rejected.why: 'ad retorquendam ueritatem' means 'to twist/distort the truth back' or 'to turn the truth against us', not 'to twist the truth' as a purpose of adding. The English makes it sound like their goal is distortion, but Latin suggests retorting/turning truth back.
last_rejected.fix: To this they add those things too, turning the truth back against us
last_rejected.ruling: ‘ad retorquendam veritatem’ reasonably rendered as ‘to twist the truth’

last_rejected.quote: they would rather be utterly extinguished than restored for punishment
last_rejected.source_quote: malunt enim extingui penitus quam ad supplicia reparari
last_rejected.why: 'malunt...quam' = prefer to be extinguished rather than be restored for punishments. The English 'prefer to be nothing...rather than to believe' misrepresents the Latin, which says they prefer extinction over restoration for punishment, not preferring non-existence over belief.
last_rejected.fix: for they prefer to be utterly extinguished rather than be restored for punishments
last_rejected.ruling: English captures ‘prefer extinction over restoration for punishment’
